prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, taking frequency metrology to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest example on the shortlist of a new measurement technique that changes what can be observed. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light-shift problem that otherwise limits trapped neutral atoms, and it lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once with long coherence. The demonstration is quantitative and unambiguous: fractional uncertainties and stabilities at the 10^-18 level, reproduced independently in Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in Japan, the US, Germany, France and elsewhere, and used in routine clock comparisons. The impact reaches well beyond the instrument, into tests of fundamental constants and Lorentz invariance, relativistic geodesy at the centimetre level, dark-matter searches, many-body physics inside the clock, and the pending redefinition of the second. The attribution is also the cleanest on the list, with two names covering the decisive idea and its record-setting realisation. Measurement precision is what limits our knowledge of the world, and this is where the limit has moved most in the past two decades.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are about novelty and overlap. The 2005 prize already honoured Hall and Hänsch for the frequency comb that makes optical clocks readable, and the 2012 prize honoured Wineland for ion-based control; a sceptic can say a lattice clock is a refinement of that lineage rather than a distinct discovery. The redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so the headline practical payoff is still pending. Attribution also has loose ends: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov and the ion-clock groups (Al+ at NIST, Yb+ at PTB) hold clocks at comparable accuracy and could argue for a place. Finally, Ye's contribution to the record-setting accuracy is large but is partly an engineering and systematic-control achievement building on Katori's concept, and the committee should decide whether it wants to credit that as invention.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the twisted bilayer graphene candidate B003 first because theory made a decisive prediction and nature answered with correlated insulating and superconducting states, while he ranks the lattice clocks only sixth, noting that Ye overlaps the comb lineage recognised in 2005 and that the redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: I take the prediction-then-discovery pattern seriously, and B003 is my first alternative. But I disagree on the comb overlap. The comb is a ruler for optical frequencies. The lattice clock is a different invention: it needs the magic-wavelength condition, a many-atom interrogation scheme and years of work on systematics to reach 10^-18. Hall and Hänsch did not do that, and the 2005 citation did not anticipate it. On timing, I think the redefinition argues for recognising the work now: the clocks already meet the criteria for redefinition and are already used in operational comparisons. My experimentalist worry about B003 is that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and the sample dependence of the superconducting phase is still being sorted out. That makes me want a few more years of consolidation, which the lattice clock does not need.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B043, circuit QED, first, but he ranks the lattice clocks third and calls the precision gain a vivid scientific signal with a fair two-person attribution. He mentions Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow as people who would come up.
responses.response: We agree on the clocks, and I appreciate that he declares his proximity to circuit QED. I would qualify the circuit QED case as follows. The physics is clear, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is recent, and awarding the same platform again so soon would need a very clean separation of the achievements. Also, the credited trio omits Wallraff, who did the first strong-coupling experiment, which makes the experimental credit weaker than for the clocks. On Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow: I accept that they matter for particular milestones. Takamoto's 2005 Sr clock and Ludlow's 2015 JILA comparison are important, but the invention and the sustained record accuracy are covered by the two proposed names, and a prize may stop at that boundary.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B003 and B023 first and second, regards the lattice clock as a clear and very important invention but a little outside his own area, and partly defers to the atomic physicists; he also asks whether the committee would see timing as helped by the pending redefinition.
responses.response: I welcome the deference, but I would not want the case to rest on the atomic physicists alone. The criteria are checkable by anyone: independent reproduction, quantitative improvement by orders of magnitude, and a new set of measurements that were not possible before. Judged by those, B024 is easy to defend. I also take his concern about prize allocation for the competing condensed-matter candidates. B023 has a real attribution problem, since Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes are not among the credited names and the HgTe prediction is theirs. B003 leaves out Cao, the first author of the experiments. B024 has no comparable gap in the supplied names, and I regard that as a real advantage when the committee must write a citation.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clocks first alongside me, and ranks cold atoms in optical lattices, B014, second, with a three-person Bloch, Greiner and Zoller prize that is fair but leaves a hard choice among four strong names.
responses.response: I agree on B024 and I agree that the allocation in B014 is hard. This is why I would not combine the two as a shared prize. I would give Esslinger more weight than Zoller on experimental grounds, but I admit that this reflects my own bias towards the lab. A configuration of three leaves out either Jaksch and Zoller as the originators of the Hubbard proposal, or one of the experimentalists. Because B014 is also close to the BEC prize of 2001 and the 2012 prize, I regard it as a good second prize candidate for a later year, but not a strong shared-prize partner for B024 now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems, or will see it as a continuation.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or the ion-clock groups have a claim strong enough to disturb a clean two-person attribution.

I did not have the opening arguments of Mehlig, Olsson or Pearce in front of me when writing this statement, so I have not responded to their specific scientific or attribution points on B001, B006 or B035 and may need to revisit these.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes the recognition better timed, or whether the committee prefers to wait until it has formally happened.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year during my doctoral work in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder. Hall shared the 2005 prize for the comb, and Jun Ye is a close colleague and former collaborator of Hall at JILA, so there is a personal and lineage connection to one credited candidate that the committee may wish to weigh when considering recusal. I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye apparent from my profile. I also work in atomic and optical physics at Lund, which may bias me toward precision atomic physics.
